The utility outcomes of cervical cancer screening strategies, compared to conservative follow-up protocols (such as observation, surveillance, and cytology-based follow-up), were assessed using various measures like Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Rating Scale (RS), and Standard Gamble (SG). For patients undergoing repeat cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy or treatment, there was a loss of 0.034 Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) based on EQ-5D, 0.27 based on VAS, and 0.03 based on Health Utilities Index (HUI). 2. A systematic review of studies using conjoint analysis and discrete-choice experiments identified key attributes that patients value in cervical cancer screening tests. These include pain during the procedure, the interval between tests, the time to receive results and treatment, diagnostic accuracy (especially the probability of false positives), the likelihood of detecting abnormalities, the chance of being recalled, the probability of dying from cancer, the cost of the test, and compliance with follow-up protocols. 3. A meta-analysis of women with histologically confirmed CIN 2 who were not treated at diagnosis but followed up with active surveillance showed varying non-compliance rates at different follow-up intervals: 4% at 3 months, 19% at 6 months, 15% at 12 months, 8% at 24 months, and 4% at 36 months. Programs offering same-day colposcopy had a non-compliance rate of 4%. 4. In Tanzania, women who tested positive for VIA but postponed treatment and did not return were often younger, resided in urban areas like Dar es Salaam, and were more likely to have skilled occupations compared to housewives. 5. Studies on HPV DNA testing algorithms revealed that just over 50% of immigrant women and those not attending routine cervical cancer screening followed up on positive HPV DNA test results. In the Netherlands, 8% of women adhered to follow-up after positive high-risk HPV screening tests with cytology and colposcopy. 6. Women living with HIV (WLHIV) are more likely to receive preventive cervical cancer screening and attend screening programs compared to HIV-negative women. Among women who tested positive for VIA in screen-and-treat programs, 68% underwent cryotherapy when treatment was provided during the same visit. Lower compliance rates were observed when women were referred for treatment or follow-up at a later date. 7. Logistical challenges, such as maintaining a consistent supply of gas for cryotherapy, can hinder the provision of treatment for women with positive VIA test results. Barriers to treatment include limited access to modern cancer therapies (e.g., chemotherapy for invasive cancer), inadequate staffing and availability of trained healthcare providers, and geographic constraints that make travel for treatment difficult, particularly in rural areas of Tanzania. 8. Factors associated with increased likelihood of attending cervical cancer screening include older age, having health insurance, prior knowledge about cervical cancer, and condom use in rural areas. Women with a poorer quality of life, those who regularly listen to the radio, or those who faced cost barriers to healthcare in the past year were also more likely to attend screening. Multiparous women, those who do not involve their spouse in health-related decisions, and those with a single lifetime sexual partner were more likely to participate in screening. 9. A significant proportion of women expressed willingness to travel over two hours to attend a screening clinic. Positive influences from significant others, healthcare providers, and screening guidelines, as well as a positive HPV vaccination status, were associated with higher screening participation. Contraceptive use, higher income, and education levels were variably associated with HPV test acceptability. 10. Negative emotions and perceptions related to HPV testing, being non-white (except Latina women), and marital status (e.g., single women) were potential barriers to HPV test acceptability. Some studies found no association between marital status and test acceptability, while others reported lower acceptability among single women. 11. Primary HPV screening strategies, particularly those without triage or with HPV 16/18 triage, were the most effective in reducing cervical cancer incidence. Testing every five years from ages 30 to 50 using primary HPV without triage (with VIA determining eligibility for same-day ablation) resulted in a 57% reduction in cancer incidence. HPV 16/18 triage achieved a 56% reduction. 12. The best balance of benefits to harms was achieved with primary HPV screening combined with triaging methods (e.g., colposcopy, VIA, or HPV 16/18). For example, HPV 16/18 triage resulted in 31% fewer precancer treatment events and 23% fewer adverse obstetric outcomes compared to primary HPV without triage. 13. Cost-effectiveness analyses showed that primary HPV without triage was the most cost-effective approach, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) of $154 per HALY saved for 10-year intervals at ages 35-45, $393 per HALY saved for 10-year intervals at ages 30-50, and $502 per HALY saved for five-year intervals at ages 30-50. However, primary HPV with 16/18 triage had similar costs and effects and offered a better balance of benefits to harms. 14. For WLHIV, more frequent screening starting at a younger age was recommended. The benefits of screening in this high-burden population were greater in magnitude than for the general population, but the associated harms were also larger. 15. Screening compliance was assumed to be 70% for routine attendance and 90% for treatment or follow-up visits. Sensitivity analyses considered scenarios with lower compliance rates (50% for routine attendance and 75% for follow-up). 16. The most effective strategies for general population women in 78 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) were primary HPV without triage and primary HPV with 16/18 triage at five-year intervals for ages 30-50. These approaches were cost-effective and provided a balanced ratio of benefits to harms compared to other screening methods.
